mcqs.question: When you encode a range covering time 2 through time 5 with a contribution of +1 as sweep-line events, which pair of events do you create?
options: A single event at time 2 with value -1
An event at time 2 with value +1 and an event at time 5 with value -1
An event at time 5 with value +1 and an event at time 2 with value -1
Two events both at time 2, one +1 and one -1
mcqs.explanation: The start of the range adds its contribution and the end removes that exact same contribution, so the running total correctly reflects only the ranges currently active. Reversing which endpoint gets which sign, or placing both events at the same timestamp, breaks the running total entirely.

mcqs.question: Why is the sweep-line technique preferred over a nested-loop scan that checks every pair of ranges for overlap?
options: It uses less memory because it never stores the ranges at all
It reduces the work from O(n²) pairwise comparisons to O(n log n) by sorting events once and scanning linearly
It guarantees a correct answer while the nested-loop approach does not
It removes the need to sort anything before scanning
mcqs.explanation: Sweep line still needs to sort the O(n) events, but that replaces an O(n²) all-pairs comparison with a single O(n log n) sort plus a linear scan. Both approaches are correct when implemented properly; the difference is purely how they scale.

mcqs.question: Two events land on the exact same timestamp: a range ending and a different range starting. What goes wrong if you sort events by time alone with no tie-break rule?
options: The sweep will throw a runtime error on duplicate timestamps
Sorting becomes O(n²) instead of O(n log n)
One of the two events will simply be dropped, undercounting the total
The end and start events can be processed in either order, silently changing whether the running total counts both ranges as simultaneously active
mcqs.explanation: With no deterministic tie-break, a sort is free to place the start before the end at that timestamp, temporarily inflating the running total by one exactly at the boundary. Sorting on (time, delta) fixes this by always processing negative deltas before positive ones at a tie, since nothing is dropped or errors out.

mcqs.question: You need to compute, for a huge but sparse set of ranges, the running total covering every point in a very large or real-valued coordinate space. When does sweep line win over a difference array?
options: Sweep line is always faster regardless of the coordinate range
A difference array is faster only when the ranges don't overlap
Sweep line requires more memory than a difference array in every case
When the coordinate range is far larger than the number of ranges — a difference array needs an array sized to the range, while sweep line only needs to sort the O(n) actual endpoints
mcqs.explanation: A difference array's cost is tied to the size of the coordinate space, which becomes infeasible for huge or continuous (timestamp, floating-point) ranges. Sweep line's cost is tied only to the number of ranges, so it stays practical exactly where a difference array can't even be allocated.

mcqs.question: A rate limiter needs to know the peak number of concurrent in-flight requests over a sliding window, given each request's start and end timestamp. Which technique fits directly?
options: Sweep line over start/end events with a running counter, tracking the maximum
A hash map counting total requests per second, summed over the window
Binary search over the sorted start times only
A greedy earliest-finish-time selection, as used in Erase Overlap Intervals
mcqs.explanation: Peak concurrent requests is exactly a peak-concurrency computation — the same start/end event sweep with a running counter used for Meeting Rooms II, just applied continuously to a live stream instead of a fixed array. Summing per-second counts or greedy removal solve different questions.
